strengths: The system addresses a relevant problem: robust monocular visual-inertial tracking combined with dense Gaussian mapping. Integrating learned dense correspondences with inertial optimization is practically useful even though many constituent techniques are established.

Evaluation spans four datasets with different environments and capture conditions. Reported average ATE improves over HI-SLAM2 from 8.10 to 3.24 cm on UTMM and from 10.22 to 6.08 cm on FAST-LIVO2. Rendering metrics also improve across all three evaluated color datasets, supported by visibly sharper details in Figure 3.

The frame-subsampling experiments provide particularly strong evidence of robustness. On EuRoC at stride 10, the method achieves 98.99% recall at 10 cm versus 28.64% for HI-SLAM2. Reporting trajectory coverage alongside ATE appropriately exposes methods that accurately track only short segments.

The evaluation excludes mapping views from rendering tests and separates online results from expensive final refinement. Component ablations support the usefulness of inertial fusion, inertial pose initialization, loop closure, and Gaussian map correction.
weaknesses: The repeated real-time claim conflicts with the supplied measurements. Table 9 reports only 16.40 FPS for tracking and 7.09 FPS for the complete system on a 30 FPS dataset, despite using an RTX 5090. Future CUDA optimization does not establish current real-time performance. This materially limits the claimed suitability for live robotics and AR applications.

The distinctive contribution is insufficiently isolated. Staged initialization, time-varying biases, and Jacobian-based preintegration corrections are established visual-inertial techniques, while the visual frontend and pose-graph machinery build directly on prior systems. Table 6 removes whole components but does not compare joint versus alternating optimization, fixed versus varying biases, or alternative initialization strategies. A matched comparison with a simpler inertial extension of the same frontend would better establish the claimed advance over prior fusion designs.

The treatment of inertial consistency after loop closure is unclear. Equation (3) performs visual and relative-pose optimization in Sim(3), but the paper explains only how poses and Gaussians are corrected. It does not explain how velocities, gravity alignment, and active inertial constraints are reconciled with keyframe-dependent scale and rotation updates. This is consequential for a tightly coupled visual-inertial system. Additionally, the velocity residual following Equation (2) includes only gyroscope-bias correction, apparently omitting accelerometer-bias dependence; whether this is a notation error or an implementation issue needs clarification.

Evaluation details leave uncertainty about metric accuracy and reproducibility. Trajectories are aligned using evo, but the alignment group and scale correction are unspecified, so the results do not clearly establish metric-scale recovery. No run-to-run variability is reported, making the small EuRoC improvement over HI-SLAM2—2.94 to 2.79 cm—difficult to interpret. There is also a concrete reporting inconsistency: the OPEN-VINS per-sequence values in Table 1 are permuted relative to Table 19 at stride 1.

The rendering comparison does not control mapping effort. Table 9 reports substantially more keyframes for the proposed method than HI-SLAM2, and mapping receives ten iterations per new keyframe. Consequently, additional mapped views and optimization may explain part of the quality gain. A matched-keyframe or matched-compute comparison would strengthen attribution to the proposed fusion. Overall, the robustness results are promising, but these unresolved technical and evidential concerns slightly outweigh the acceptance case.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: robust monocular tracking with photorealistic Gaussian mapping under degraded visual input. Integrating dense learned correspondences with inertial constraints is well motivated, and the principal inherited methods are acknowledged.

Evaluation spans four datasets and includes substantial robustness gains. On EuRoC at stride 10, VIGS-SLAM achieves 3.39 cm average ATE and 98.99% recall@10cm, compared with 144.43 cm and 28.64% for HI-SLAM2. Recall appropriately exposes methods that achieve low ATE only on short tracked segments.

Mapping results improve across the three color datasets. Before final refinement, PSNR improves over HI-SLAM2 by approximately 1–2 dB, with accompanying SSIM and LPIPS gains and visually sharper examples in Figure 3.

The separation of online results from expensive final refinement is valuable. The supplement provides detailed per-sequence results, implementation thresholds, runtime measurements, and ablations demonstrating the benefits of IMU fusion, keyframe initialization, and Gaussian updates after loop closure.
weaknesses: The repeated real-time claim is contradicted by the reported measurements. Table 9 shows only 16.40 FPS for tracking and 7.09 FPS for the complete system on an RTX 5090, whereas RPNG supplies 30 FPS imagery. No bounded-latency streaming demonstration resolves this discrepancy. Anticipated CUDA optimization is future work, not evidence for the current claim.

Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the specific methodological advance is insufficiently isolated. Dense correspondence estimation, IMU preintegration with bias correction, staged initialization, pose-graph optimization, and Gaussian mapping largely build on established components. This integration can still be valuable, but Table 6 does not test joint versus alternating optimization, fixed versus time-varying biases, or staged versus alternative initialization—the distinctions emphasized against prior visual-inertial Gaussian systems. It also does not establish that keyframe selection and mapping budgets are matched when assessing the gains.

Consistency between inertial estimation and loop closure is underexplained. Equation (3) optimizes a Sim(3) graph using visual and relative-pose constraints, but the paper describes subsequent corrections only for camera poses and Gaussians. It does not explain how velocities, gravity, and retained inertial constraints remain consistent after spatially varying rotation and scale corrections. This is material to the claimed unified visual-inertial system.

The evaluation protocol does not specify whether trajectory alignment uses SE(3) or Sim(3), despite metric-scale recovery being an important motivation. Scale-preserving trajectory errors and explicit scale-error measurements are needed to establish that benefit. FAST-LIVO2 trajectories are transparently identified as pseudo ground truth, but their uncertainty is not quantified, limiting interpretation of centimeter-level outdoor differences.

Comparative evidence has unresolved reliability issues. No repeated-run variability is reported, although the full-rate EuRoC improvement over HI-SLAM2 is only 2.94 to 2.79 cm. Moreover, the OPEN-VINS per-sequence values in Table 1 are permuted relative to the stride-1 results in Table 19, despite an identical average. Comparisons mix reproduced and published results, and the principal contrast with VINGS-Mono remains qualitative rather than experimentally controlled.

Important implementation details remain missing, including the local-window and marginalization policy, visual–inertial weighting/calibration, and mapping loss weights. The velocity residual following Equation (2) includes only gyroscope-bias correction, apparently omitting accelerometer-bias dependence; this may be a notation error but requires clarification. Together with the unresolved consistency and evaluation questions, these gaps prevent a sufficiently convincing acceptance case despite the promising empirical results.

strengths: The paper presents a useful integration of dense learned visual correspondences, joint visual-inertial bundle adjustment, and Gaussian mapping. Although the individual ingredients are largely established, their combination addresses a practical weakness of visual Gaussian SLAM under degraded observations.

Evaluation spans four datasets with varied environments and capture platforms. Tracking improvements are substantial on UTMM (3.24 cm versus HI-SLAM2’s 8.10 cm average ATE) and FAST-LIVO2 (6.08 versus 10.22 cm). Rendering metrics improve across all three evaluated RGB datasets, supported by the qualitative comparisons in Figure 3.

The frame-subsampling experiments provide strong evidence of robustness. On EuRoC at stride 10, the method achieves 98.99% recall at 10 cm versus 28.64% for HI-SLAM2. Reporting trajectory coverage alongside ATE appropriately exposes methods that obtain low errors only on short tracked segments.

The ablations demonstrate meaningful contributions from IMU fusion, inertial keyframe initialization, loop closure, and Gaussian correction. Separating online results from expensive final refinement, evaluating rendering on common non-keyframes, and providing detailed supplementary results improve the experimental case. Overall, these practical benefits support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The repeated real-time claim is contradicted by the reported measurements. Table 9 gives 16.40 FPS for tracking and 7.09 FPS for the full system on an RTX 5090, while RPNG input runs at 30 FPS. Anticipated CUDA improvements are not evidence of current performance. The claims should be narrowed, and latency or backlog under live input should be measured.

The algorithmic novelty is limited and insufficiently isolated. Staged initialization, time-varying biases, preintegration corrections, DROID-style correspondence optimization, and HI-SLAM2-inspired pose-graph optimization build on established techniques. The ablations remove broad components but do not test the claimed advantages of joint versus alternating fusion, variable versus fixed biases, or staged initialization. A matched comparison against a simpler fusion design would better establish the contribution.

Inertial consistency after loop closure is underspecified. Equation (3) optimizes a Sim(3) graph without inertial terms, but the paper does not explain how per-keyframe scale and rotation corrections propagate to velocities, gravity, and the active inertial optimization. Updating Gaussian means and covariances establishes map alignment but does not establish consistency of the complete visual-inertial state.

The trajectory evaluation needs greater precision: the manuscript does not specify SE(3) versus Sim(3) alignment, scale correction, or the timestamp association/interpolation used for recall. This matters especially for a method claiming metric-scale recovery and for comparisons under frame subsampling. FAST-LIVO2 results measure agreement with a reference estimator rather than independent ground truth. Repeated-run variability is also absent, making the small EuRoC improvement over HI-SLAM2 (2.79 versus 2.94 cm) difficult to assess.

Some technical and reporting details require correction. The velocity residual in Section 3.1 includes only gyroscope-bias correction, omitting the accelerometer-bias dependence expected in velocity preintegration; it is unclear whether this is merely a notation error. The OpenVINS sequence entries in Table 1 are also permuted relative to Table 19 despite having the same average. These issues should be resolved for reliable reproduction.
